text:
marco: Heads-up — noticed a long tail on GPU pod Pending in eu-west this morning. ~90% of scale-ups were fine but ~10% took 6–9m to become Ready. Looks like API throttling + image pull/startup scripts chewing time.

anya: Ugh. Any event snippets or node provisioning logs?

marco: Pasted the relevant events we saw:
```
Warning  FailedScheduling  5m   default-scheduler  0/10 nodes are available: 10 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu.
Normal   TriggeredScaleUp   5m   cluster-autoscaler  pod triggered scale-up: group=gpu-spot-eu-west, size: 3 -> 6
Normal   StartedInstanceProvision  4m  cloud-controller  Creating instance for node pool gpu-spot-eu-west (req: 3)
Warning  ThrottledRequests 3m  cloud-provider   Throttled requests to compute.googleapis.com (quota exceeded)
Normal   NodeCreated  2m  kubelet  Node node-gpu-xyz created, waiting for kubelet register
Normal   NodeReady  0m  kubelet  Node node-gpu-xyz is Ready
```

dinesh: That ThrottledRequests line is the smoking gun. When the cloud API starts queuing, instance creation spreads out and our "fast" scale-up becomes a slow trickle. Two levers here: reduce parallel creates and/or pre-warm nodes. Also watch imagePull times (private registry).

katie: Agreed. Proposal: add a soft ramp policy and tweak CA flags for canary first:
- Reduce simultaneous provisioning per nodepool (cloud provider > quota) by rate-limiting scale-ups in config (see example below).
- Set --max-node-provision-time=12m (was 15m) so CA gives up earlier on hung creates and tries alternatives.
- Use --expander=most-pods for GPU pools to prefer denser packing of GPUs.
- Increase --scan-interval to 15s to smooth decisions (was 5s).
- Expose metric NodeProvisionTime and an alert at 4m median over 10m.

marco: That sounds reasonable. How do we implement the per-nodepool parallelism? We don't want CA to burst 5-10 creates at once in a region.

anya: We can graft a small controller that tracks outstanding creates per nodepool and annotates the NodeGroup object to temporarily mark the group as "paused" for CA to avoid further creates, or use CA's 'max-empty-bulk' style logic (if available). Short-term: tweak cloud autoscaler config to limit max total simultaneous node creations to 3 in eu-west.

katie: Example CA args (canary):
```yaml
args:
  - --cloud-provider=gce
  - --expander=most-pods
  - --max-node-provision-time=12m
  - --scan-interval=15s
  - --max-total-unready-percentage=40
```
Also add a small Deployment for a "scale-ramp-controller" with these heuristics: per-nodepool counter + cooldown.

dinesh: Another operational option: keep a 1-node warm buffer during peak hours per GPU pool (min-size = configured-min + 1) and use pod priorities to evict when not needed. Cost impact is predictable and might be cheaper than long tails.

marco: Do we have cost estimate for warm buffer? Rough math: 3 pools * 1 p3-equivalent * 24/30 = ~0.9k/mo (quick calc). Worth trial for top 2 pools.

anya: Also check kubelet tune: kubelet --node-status-update-frequency and K8s cluster-autoscaler node readiness probes. Slow cloud-init or startup scripts often dominate. Make init scripts smaller, cache images, and enable registry pull concurrency.

sre-bot: ALERT: autoscaler-slow-scaleup eu-west triggered 1975012341 (NodeProvisionTime > 6m for 3 nodes).

marco: Next steps: 1) I'll open a canary PR with CA arg changes + ramp controller prototype. 2) Dinesh / Anya to run image/boot time profiling on a sample node. 3) Katie to draft runbook and cost calc for 1-node warm buffer. 4) We'll monitor NodeProvisionTime metric and cloud API quota. Plan to test for 48h in canary cluster before rolling to prod.

katie: SGTM :thumbsup:

anya: Adding a note — if throttling persists, we should consider spreading node pools across two regions (eu-west + eu-north) for burst isolation. That's more complex but scales.

marco: Thanks all — I'll post PR link here when ready.
